description: A user signs up, logs back in, and reads their own data with the session they were handed. The same spec then drives ADR 0008 across the seam: a licence key is a giftable bearer claim that unlocks exactly one active account. The lane's Gumroad stub keys the sale on the licence key, so a second signup presenting the same key under another email is refused with the generic invalid_license and never learns the key was valid; deleting the first account through DELETE /users/me erases the binding (the receipt names licensebinding) and one new account then redeems the same key, inheriting access and nothing else; a third attempt is refused again. Backend suites prove the atomicity and the byte-identical refusals with an in-process client; this is the one place the production client, the Postgres UNIQUE constraint on gumroad_sale_id and the deletion cascade are exercised together. One journey rather than two because the ledger lets a spec cover exactly one journey.

A user who cannot log in asks for a reset from ForgotPasswordScreen, reads the email that arrives, follows the https link a browser can actually open, sets a new password on ResetPasswordScreen, and logs in with it; the "this wasn't me" arm cancels the token instead. This is the journey the outage came through: reset mail went to a production log for one reason and carried nothing but an adepthood:// deep link for another, and the endpoint answered 202 through both while every backend suite stayed green. The spec reads the plaintext token out of the rendered body and out of nowhere else, anchored on the https origin APP_BASE_URL configured, so a body that offered only the deep link fails it. The lane reaches that body by booting the server with EMAIL_BACKEND=capture, an adapter that appends every rendered message verbatim to a file and refuses to be built at all when ENV names production.

A user logs in and is handed a session that lives thirty days rather than an hour (#2804); a refresh rotates it, the rotated token reads their data, and the token rotated away is refused on the very next call even though its exp is weeks out. The backend suite asserts the minted lifetime and the revocation row in-process; this is the place the production client's refresh call, the jti revocation `/auth/refresh` writes, and the lookup every authenticated route performs are exercised together across the wire. The half-life renewal the client schedules against that lifetime is a timer, so it stays in the Jest suite for AuthContext.

A new account meets the intro walkthrough, pages through it, and Begin -- or Skip -- hands them to the Journal shelf, which loads the entries they do not have yet. Uncovered because this lane runs on the node environment with node_modules untransformed and cannot mount a screen at all, the same constraint recorded on errors.boundary-recovers-and-reports. The walkthrough's dismissal is a local flag rather than a request, so the only seam a spec here could watch is the shelf's own fetch, which cannot tell that the arrival came from Begin. Covering it needs a second, rendering lane, not another spec here.
A user creates a habit, checks in against one of its goals, and sees the streak move.

A user creates a subtractive habit that began today and has not logged the behavior. The server classifies the three-goal habit by the shared any-goal polarity rule and reports a one-day abstention streak; after a real reload, the Habits tile shows 1 DAYS — ACHIEVED TODAY!, because zero behavior is both a no-log streak day and within the clear ceiling. The browser runs in the user's America/Los_Angeles timezone, so the create/load round-trip also exercises the local calendar boundary rather than reparsing the server's date as UTC midnight.

A regular program habit appears when the program's invitation reaches it. A habit sitting on one of the ten rings waits for that ring to open -- its stage entering the range the calendar and the record between them have unlocked -- and a start date already in the past does not stand in for that (issue #2765: on an established account every start date is past, which opened every ring at once and stopped graduated unlock from tracking the user's level). A habit whose stage names no ring has no rung to wait for, so its start date is still its whole schedule. The habits list read persists the invitation as revealed exactly once; if the person then re-locks it, another read respects the decline instead of re-opening it. The server owns eligibility and its private marker, while the client renders only the reconciled revealed flag. Carryover habits and unrecommitted Metta Return releases remain outside this automatic path, and rows stamped before the stage gate was corrected are left open rather than retroactively re-locked, all pinned by the backend API suite.

A newly registered person whose live habits request succeeds with an empty collection sees an honest first-use state with an Add a habit action, never the fictional names, streaks, or completion history reserved for an explicitly configured demo build. The real-wire spec proves the fresh account and production client receive an empty Page; habitManager.test.ts pins that the service preserves the empty list, and HabitsEmptyState.test.tsx pins the rendered CTA.

A check-in tapped while the device is offline is queued on the device, and the next habits load replays that queue: an entry the server will never accept is dropped so the queue keeps draining behind it, while a dropped connection re-queues the unposted suffix intact. Uncovered because the real-wire lane cannot put the device offline and then make the server permanently reject a queued entry -- the constraint already recorded on errors.server-fault-is-not-offline, where no reachable failure can be manufactured without adding fault injection to the production app. Covering it needs a lane that can toggle connectivity and read the device queue. A dropped entry is also written to a bounded on-device quarantine (the most recent records only) and surfaced on the Habits screen as a count of the check-ins that could not be saved, dismissable by the user and wiped on logout, so the loss is no longer silent. The classification is pinned meanwhile by unit tests in src/features/Habits/services/__tests__/habitManager.test.ts and src/features/Habits/hooks/__tests__/useHabitActions.test.tsx, and the notice by src/features/Habits/components/__tests__/DroppedCheckInNotice.test.tsx.

In a build explicitly configured with EXPO_PUBLIC_HABIT_DEMO_MODE=true, with the habits fetch failing and no real cache, the app seeds ten demo placeholder tiles carrying fabricated ids 1-10, and those numbers are also the ids of whatever real rows the caller happens to own. A successful empty response never enters this mode. Every action on such a tile is local: revealing, reordering, renaming, changing the icon, resetting the start date, editing a goal or its shared units, logging a unit, opening stats, and -- the destructive one -- deleting. The tile changes or disappears in the store and nothing goes out, so a placeholder delete cannot become a DELETE against the user's own habit 3, and no "Couldn't sync" alert appears for something the user did only to themselves. A mixed store still performs each of those operations against the one genuinely server-backed row. Uncovered because the real-wire lane cannot produce the state -- it needs an explicitly demo-configured bundle and the habits fetch to throw while the cache is empty, while the lane's premise is a backend it can reach, the same constraint already recorded on habits.offline-check-in-replay-drains and errors.server-fault-is-not-offline. The same local-only rule covers every client-minted row, not just the demo family: onboarding scaffold rows and pre-sync added rows are marked hasClientMintedIds and may not put their provisional ids on the wire. A client-minted row is the user's real data, so it reaches the on-disk cache while a demo tile never does. Pinned meanwhile by unit tests in src/features/Habits/services/__tests__/serverIds.test.ts, src/features/Habits/services/__tests__/habitManager.test.ts, and src/features/Habits/hooks/__tests__/useHabitActions.test.tsx.

A habit added after onboarding takes the next rung on the program cadence rather than the day it was added, so the row sits where a reorder pass would put it and the date on its tile is the date its stage badge has always implied. The second half is the one that moved other screens: a row stamped today could undercut a start date the user picked in the future, because when no anchor is stored -- after a logout wipes it, or for an account that onboarded before the anchor existed -- the universal anchor Map, Practice, Course and Journal all read is re-derived as the minimum over program rows, and a today-stamped add won that minimum. Uncovered because this lane runs on the node environment with node_modules untransformed and cannot mount a screen at all, the same constraint already recorded on welcome.first-run-walkthrough-to-journal and habits.scaffolding-start-date-anchors-the-program: driving this journey means opening the add-habit sheet and reading the date on the tile it creates, and while the POST /habits/ body does carry the start_date, observing only that would not prove the user sees the rung, which is the half that regressed. Pinned meanwhile by unit tests in src/features/Habits/services/__tests__/habitManager.test.ts (the "addHabit lays a program row on the cadence" block, which covers the stored anchor, the absent-anchor fallback, the day-one case, the carryover partition, the reload that follows the add, and the saturation past ten stages that this deliberately shares with the reorder modal).

The date the user picks in Energy Scaffolding is the day their program begins, and it stays that day. They choose it in the reorder step, the scaffold rows POST with dates laid out from it, and the reload that follows re-derives the universal anchor that Map, Practice, Course and Journal all read for the current stage and week. A habit the user brought along from before the program carries the date they actually started it, which is usually earlier than the date they picked, and it must not become the program's beginning -- otherwise bringing one habit along on day one moves every other screen back to a day the program had not started. Uncovered because this lane runs on the node environment with node_modules untransformed and cannot mount a screen at all, the same constraint already recorded on welcome.first-run-walkthrough-to-journal: driving this journey means opening the scaffolding modal, operating its date picker, and adding a habit from the carryover lap, none of which a lane that cannot render can do. Pinned meanwhile by unit tests in src/features/Habits/services/__tests__/habitManager.test.ts (the "program anchor ignores carryover habits" block, which covers the live load, the offline cache, and the reload that follows onboardingSave) and by the picker's own label in src/features/Habits/components/__tests__/OnboardingModal.step4.test.tsx. Two anchors exist and this journey watches only the client's: the server stamps its own when the progress row is created, so a user who picks a future date has one of each and they disagree until they are reconciled.

A user opens Reorder Habits and performs a real browser pointer drag across the visible carryover/program boundary. Crossing that line changes the persisted is_carryover classification; after saving, the browser walks both pages and verifies that the remaining program habit keeps the ranked Beige stage color while the moved carryover tile and its progress use the unranked Candle & Ink accent. The component suite separately pins light/dark accents, achieved-state brightening, the -10 to -1, 1–10, and later-lap markers, plus program-date recalculation and carryover-date preservation.
A user writes a journal entry, finds it in the list, and reads the body back unchanged.

A writer sees that ordinary New entry still opens without a title, closes it, then takes the morning-pages invitation. The real browser lands on a fresh JournalEntry titled with that account/browser's local YYYY-MM-DD plus Daily Journal, and the writer can immediately replace the generated title. The shelf component test pins the exact prefillTitle navigation parameter, the tip test freezes a UTC instant across the prior-day America/Los_Angeles boundary, and the saved Journaling-practice quick-launch suite pins the same shared title contract.

A writer enters the journal's lightweight Markdown dialect, finishes the page, and sees asterisk-delimited bold text, underscore-delimited italics, and consecutive > lines as one quote block. The same rendering survives a cold reload while the exact source remains stored for editing and for code-point-based marginalia and promoted-quote anchors. The browser spec crosses the real editor, create/read routes, semantic web elements, and durable journal row; component coverage separately pins malformed text, literal HTML-looking prose, Unicode offsets, and anchors that cross hidden markers.

A writer types a fresh page and presses the always-available X before its debounced first save. The close waits for the create response before navigation lets the shelf refetch, the new page is visible immediately, and reopening it shows the exact body. A component regression test separately holds the create promise open to prove navigation ordering and verifies a rejected final write leaves the writer with the retry affordance.

A writer opens a fresh Journal page whose title occupies one line before they type. A long title can still wrap visually, pasted line breaks collapse to spaces, and Return moves the caret into the body without becoming stored title data. Closing crosses the production client and create route, and the returned durable row carries the exact single-line title; schema tests separately pin the server-side defence for non-UI create and update callers.

A reader opens a finished entry, uses a real mouse selection to promote part of its text, sees the saved highlight after a cold reload, and removes it again. The journey crosses the rendered selection affordance, production promotions client, ownership-scoped routes, and durable quote row instead of proving the API in isolation.

A due reflection is opened from the Journal shelf, saved with its hierarchical identity, closed, and reopened as an ordinary saved entry. Its Sources affordance survives that reopen; selecting a pending promoted quote folds it into the body, autosaves the reflection, and marks the quote included on the server.
A writer deletes one page from the shelf, the server stops serving it, and another account cannot delete it for them.

A writer whose Personal page and generated Voice Draft have reached their connected Creek vault deletes that page. The first content-free Voice Draft retraction fails at the real HTTP boundary, so Adepthood answers with its stable retryable withdrawal message and keeps the page visible instead of claiming success while derived plaintext remains. Repeating the same action after Creek recovers confirms both the AI-attributed draft and journal replica are absent before the local page disappears. The lane uses the production client and an out-of-process contract fake that records only opaque ids, tiers, actions, and digests; no journal or generated prose returns through its control surface.

Someone in the middle of a stage opens the Journal shelf and sees that stage's whole prompt set, each with the cadence the curriculum states for it, then taps one and writes against that prompt rather than against whichever question the week happened to draw. The seam is the ordinal: the page carries prompt_ordinal into the respond call, and the server decides whether that ordinal is one the stage actually carries. The second seam is the one-response-per-week rule: uq_promptresponse_user_week means a week holds a single response whichever prompt it answers, so the shelf stops offering a tap once this week's is written and the entry page says so if a save is refused anyway. Uncovered because no lane spec talks to the prompts routes yet, and a mocked client agrees with itself about the ordinal check, the stage's unlock gate, and the unique constraint -- the three things only the server can refuse.

A writer opens a page they finished days ago, asks for its resonance, and the reading lands in the margin against the words they actually wrote. The unhappy half is part of the journey rather than an edge case: a pass can legitimately keep nothing -- the model declines, or every quote it offers is a paraphrase that will not anchor -- and what the writer must never get is the outcome that was reported here, a button that visibly does nothing. So the journey ends either in a persisted note or in a sentence saying why there is none, with the charge reversed. Both endings are driven here against the configured default provider, which is the stub (BOTMASON_PROVIDER unset: no key, no network, no third party), so the route, the wallet, the anchoring and the rows are all real and only the model's sentences are canned; the stub declines exactly when the page gives it no sentence to copy, which is how the lane reaches the second ending. The spec also pins the privacy floor across the wire: an intimate page is answered before any provider is constructed, keeps no notes, and is not charged. What is NOT claimed is that any of it renders -- this lane runs on the node environment with node_modules untransformed and cannot mount JournalEntryScreen at all, the constraint recorded on welcome.first-run-walkthrough-to-journal. The margin's placement and its empty-state copy stay pinned by the Jest specs beside the screen; what crosses the seam here is that the note the margin will draw is one the server kept, anchored to characters the writer wrote.

A writer opens a finished page and presses Get Resonance for the first time. The press opens a disclosure before any request leaves the browser: what a pass does, that the entry's text is sent to an AI model, and who pays. With no key, the rendered copy uses the deployment-served monthly cap and never promises that the allowance is free. The writer backs out, saves their own key through Settings, reopens the same page, and now sees that the key pays and neither BotMason bucket will move. Continue sends exactly one real request through the screen and production API to the lane's provider; its deterministic credit refusal proves the BYOK header arrived, while GET /user/usage proves both BotMason buckets stayed unchanged. The dismissal is then taken and the next press goes straight through without silently switching payer. Counted requests and server state keep the journey non-vacuous: a dialog-only assertion could pass while charging too early or charging both payers. This has to be the browser lane because the claim spans rendered presses and device key storage. Per-account namespacing of the dismissal flag remains pinned in the Jest specs beside the screen.

A writer can open API-key settings from the journal entry's exit row and return to the exact editor with its title and body intact. When the account has neither a monthly message nor an offering and no device key, Get Resonance opens a refill invitation naming the reset date instead of a disabled spend disclosure; its Add your API key arm reaches the same settings screen and returns without losing the draft. A second browser account makes the usage read stale, takes and dismisses the ordinary spend disclosure, and receives a real-shaped 402 from the pass: the refill invitation still replaces the old dialog, proving the dismissal flag cannot suppress the recovery path. A third holds the initial wallet response while the writer uses the live Settings form to save a lane key, then proves the mounted entry publishes only the new BYOK payer when that obsolete zero-wallet response arrives. A fourth holds an accepted resonance POST, opens and saves API-key settings, then releases a key-required 402 and proves the obsolete request cannot portal a funding invitation over Settings or the preserved entry. The browser intercepts only the deterministic wallet arrangements and funding failures; navigation, editor state, key storage/context, modal decisions, API client parsing, and request count all run through production code.

A writer asks for resonance on a short saved entry that explicitly says they completed a tracked habit. The literary pass is refused at the browser boundary, but the production client still runs its independent completion check against the live server, renders both an honest reflection error and the habit offer, and accepting the offer persists the check-in. The literary refusal is deterministic route interception; detection, suggestion persistence, acceptance, and completion are real-wire behavior.

A writer asks for resonance and, when their connected Creek vault recognises a compiled praxis or a recurring eddy in the entry, finds those related pages offered in a collapsed, display-only band beside the journal page. Expanding it shows the page titles, quiet lifecycle or fragment context, and excerpts without turning a pattern into a task. Empty and pre-vault responses leave no band behind. The reflection provider is no longer what blocks this: the lane's default provider now answers a resonance ask with an anchored reading, which is what journal.ask-for-resonance drives. What is still missing is the other half of the response -- a Creek vault fake, connected to the account and seeded with compiled praxis and eddy pages, that answers the reflection with related collections. The activation journey's fake Creek control plane allocates a vault; it does not serve a corpus. The component, hook, and rendered-screen contracts are pinned by the Jest specs beside JournalEntryScreen, and #2408 stays open for this seeded-vault seam.

A writer who has never decided about their corpus asks for resonance on a finished page and, once the reflection has actually landed in the margin, finds beside the page -- never in it -- a quiet note saying reflections can draw on their own earlier writing, what agreeing sends where and how often, and that a yes also sorts what is already written. They can look at the decision, set it aside with Not now, or say Do not ask again; every one of those is one tap, none of them touches the pass, and the answer is kept on the server so it holds across devices and does not return on the next press. On a plain Not now the note returns only after both seven days and three further completed passes; on Do not ask again, or once consent is decided either way, never. The pass count the cooldown runs on never reaches the client. Uncovered as a rendered moment: this journey is about the note appearing beside the page after the pass, and the real-wire lane drives the production client, not the screen. The wire half -- a completed pass opening the offer, and the decline being the server's to remember -- is covered by corpus.decline-the-offer-and-be-left-alone; the rendered half is pinned by the Jest specs beside JournalEntryScreen (placement, one-tap decline, the pass never gated) and by backend/tests/test_resonance_endpoints.py::TestACompletedPassIsCounted for which passes count. The provider seam is no longer what blocks it -- journal.ask-for-resonance now drives a pass that keeps real notes against the default stub provider, and this journey's remaining gap is only the rendered moment, which needs a lane that can mount the screen. #2408 stays open for it rather than being closed by the spec that covered the pass.

A writer who has never decided about their corpus completes a first resonance pass and is offered the decision; they set it aside with Not now and are not asked again on the very next pass; later they say Do not ask again, and a softer Not now afterwards does not undo it. A cold login on a fresh session reads the same standing, because the decision is the server's to remember rather than the device's; a request with no session is refused; and a neighbour's account is still un-asked until its own first pass opens its own offer. The pass that opens the offer is real -- the lane's provider is the stub, so it resolves as a refunded no-notes 200, which is still a completed pass by design -- so the seam this spec pins is the whole of it: the settlement counting the pass, the read the note makes, the verb and shape of both declines, and that the count itself never crosses the wire. Both halves are green on their own -- the note's tests mock the client, the router's tests never see it -- and this is the one place they agree.
A practitioner logs a practice session and finds it in the week's record.
A practitioner who sat without the app logs that sitting afterwards, choosing when it ended and how long it ran, and finds it counted in the week it happened.

A practitioner runs the stage-1 grounding ritual to its end, saves it with a one-line insight, and watches the weekly bar move from 0 of 4 to 1 of 4 in the page they are already looking at. The bar was wired correctly on both sides and still showed the pre-save number: the client incremented optimistically and then refetched, the server counted the new row, and in between GET /practice-sessions/insights advertised max-age=60, so the browser answered the post-save refetch out of its own HTTP cache and put the bar back to zero. No node-lane spec can see that -- node's fetch keeps no HTTP cache, so the request the browser answers for itself is the one the node lane always puts on the wire. This journey runs in the Playwright lane against a real server for exactly that reason, and asserts the server's own week-count alongside the rendered number so a failure separates a lost save from a display that lies about one.

A practitioner who has sat one practice several times walks from the player to that practice's own detail screen -- Practice, its drawer, "Practice details" -- and reads how much they have put into it: total sittings and total time, rendered as hours plus the minutes past 60. The totals are a backend aggregate keyed on an adoption the caller owns, never a client-side sum over a paged session list, and the aggregate widens server-side to every adoption of the same catalog practice that caller owns, so a practice carried from one stage into the next reports one lifetime figure rather than a per-stage slice. The spec logs a zero-length abort alongside two real sittings and asserts it moves neither number, which is the counting rule this endpoint had to settle: the insights rollup skips zero-duration rows, the legacy week-count route does not, and a total cannot honour both. It runs in the Playwright lane because the node lane cannot mount a screen at all (#2324), and because the rollup is read one tap from the player that writes the rows it counts -- the #2654 hazard, which only a browser holding an HTTP cache can see, so the last leg leaves the screen and comes back to force a real re-read.
A practitioner submits a custom practice and adopts it as one they can actually do.

A reader opens a stage's content, reads a piece, and marks it read so progress moves. Which stage it opens on is the server's answer, not a count of completed stages the client makes for itself. The cold start's bounded wait is a state of this journey, not a journey of its own: it crosses no screen, client wrapper, route or table this entry does not already name -- it is a client-side timer over the same GET /stages read, and it is reached precisely when that read never answers, which no lane against a live server can arrange. Pinned in-process by src/features/Course/__tests__/CourseScreenColdStart.test.tsx, the way the Map's identical bounded wait is pinned by MapScreenColdStart.test.tsx and declared nowhere in this ledger.

A reader in a desktop browser opens a chapter, chooses Write a note on a passage, selects a passage by keyboard, double-click, and pointer drag, confirms Write a note, lands in JournalEntry with the passage prefilled as a blockquote, and waits for the entry to save. The covering Playwright spec boots the real Expo web app and FastAPI app over loopback against an alembic-built throwaway Postgres database; it exists because the Node API lane cannot exercise native textarea selection or browser accessibility semantics.

A reader finishes a chapter, marks it read, and taps Reflect in Journal. The writing surface opens already titled for the stage and the chapter, the reflection saves, and the way out is the way in: Back to reading returns them to that same chapter instead of leaving them on the Journal shelf to find the Course tab by hand. Sibling to course.write-note-on-passage, which drives the reader's other hand-off; this one is the reflection, which closes the reader behind it and so returns to the chapter rather than to a scroll position. It runs in the browser lane because the whole journey is screen-to-screen navigation -- the returnTo that makes the exit exist never crosses the wire, so no amount of API driving could see whether it is there. Verified to be a live gate rather than a passing formality: with the returnTo removed from handleReflect the spec fails on the absent Back to reading control.

A user whose first page of habits is full opens Habits in a desktop browser and, after a viewport flip to a phone profile, in one column. The covering Playwright spec signs up through the UI, seeds ten habits over POST /habits/ with a token from POST /auth/login, and then measures laid-out DOM: the grid's box ends at or above the top of both the pagination bar and the Energy Scaffolding CTA, and every tile lies inside the grid's box -- the first before any scrolling, the last after scrolling the grid to its end. It exists because the Jest lanes cannot answer a layout question at all: this project runs the node environment under the React Native preset, so onLayout never fires and every box is zero, which is why issue #2658's report of a grid "clipped beneath fixed controls" survived a green suite. Nothing here asserts that a full page fits without scrolling; the same spec measured 147px of overflow at 1280x720 and 129px at 390x844, and records those numbers on every run instead of claiming a fit the app does not hold.

A traveller opens the Map after the calendar has moved them into a new stage, and the server agrees they moved. Advance is not an action a person takes: the calendar over the ratified 21x8+42x2 schedule decides what is offered, and reading the Map records that the person entered it. There is deliberately no tap affordance -- a manual advance contradicts the earned, server-derived progression model -- so the covering spec moves the program anchor in the lane's own database and then reads, never posts. The three reads below are the whole of what the Map asks for: GET /stages/{stage_number}/progress is served but unreachable, and naming it here described a seam the app has no half of. Unlocking alone would prove nothing, because access is the union of the calendar and the record; so the spec asserts the record itself -- current_stage, completed_stages, stage_started_at -- moved when the Map was read, stayed put when the anchor moved without a read, and re-recorded nothing on a second read inside the same window.

A traveller opens the current stage on the Map and takes its strongest action, Continue, directly into that stage's Course chapter. The stage modal offers Course exactly once through that primary action; Practice and Journal occupy the two secondary slots, so no destination is duplicated. The component journey separately pins the stage-number route parameter and the close-before-navigation/double-tap guard, while this real-browser journey proves the rendered accessibility name, action hierarchy, modal dismissal, tab hand-off, and selected Course cover together.

Someone turns a depth ring on or off and the app they come back to is the one they chose: Habits, Practice and Course each add or remove their primary destination; Sangha adds or removes the Digital Sangha door in Settings (SanghaSection.tsx), and its switch is offered only in a build with EXPO_PUBLIC_SANGHA_INVITE_URL configured, because a switch with nothing to close would be a false choice. The live-wire spec proves enable_sangha round-trips independently; the in-process pairing of each switch with its destination is pinned by src/features/Settings/__tests__/depthSwitchesHaveEffect.test.tsx.

A person who HAS connected a vault chooses a document from their device and seeds it there; the import forwards to the vault rather than persisting locally, so authentication is the only table it crosses. One route serves both destinations -- POST /corpus/import decides per account -- and this entry is the vault half of that decision, the corpus half being corpus.import-without-a-vault. The lane now has a vault to reach: a loopback process answering Creek's published GET /v1/capabilities and POST /v1/uploads, reached through adepthood's own production CREEK_VAULT_URL and bound to one pre-provisioned account by CREEK_VAULT_OWNER_USER_ID. That binding is what closed the last blocker -- the variable is read from the server's environment and so names an id fixed before any account exists, which globalSetup settles by signing that account up as the lane's first request and refusing the whole run if the id it gets back is not the one already named. The deployment-wide value is also the only one that may name loopback: a user-supplied vault URL is refused unless it names a globally routable destination, which is why the connect-your-own path cannot serve this. The spec proves the seam end to end -- accepted with a ref, a re-send reported as one fragment edited in place rather than a second, and an Intimate document withheld before the vault is contacted at all, asserted against the vault's own record of what arrived.

Someone who has connected no vault brings in a document they wrote elsewhere: they pick it, choose its tier, and it is routed to their own ontologized corpus rather than answered in the vocabulary of a vault they do not have. The first answer is the consent question, because the corpus is off until they turn it on; the screen offers the way to that switch instead of failing silently. A format nothing can read is refused before consent is even consulted, and an Intimate document is declined outright -- placing writing among the frequencies means reading it with a language model, and that tier never goes to one. The stored outcome itself needs a classification call, which the lane has no provider for, so a consented import settles there as unclassified.

Someone brings in a batch and leaves the screen before it has all gone over. The screen asks first rather than silently discarding the run, and confirming genuinely stops it: the document already in flight finishes wherever it lands, and everything still queued is never sent. The point of the journey is the seam, not the prompt -- what has to be proved is that the account's corpus afterwards holds exactly the documents that had settled on screen, because the defect this closes was a run that kept uploading in the background while the person saw an empty screen. Covered at the hook and screen level by Jest (useSeedRun, useSeedLeaveGuard, SeedCorpusScreen), which can only assert that the client stopped calling the route; uncovered here because no spec yet reads the corpus back to confirm the server agrees.

Someone takes a copy of everything they have written: they open Export my data, the app downloads the JSON archive and the Markdown journal, saves both to the device and offers them to the share sheet. The archive carries their own entries as prose, never another account's, and never the ciphertext the column holds.

Someone saves their own OpenAI or Anthropic key on the device, then uses a model-powered feature. The production app sends the key over HTTPS to Adepthood in the X-LLM-API-Key header, and Adepthood forwards it over HTTPS to the selected provider for that request without persisting, logging, or returning it. Both Settings surfaces disclose those two service boundaries before the key is used. The copy and wire contract are pinned together by src/features/Settings/__tests__/byokDisclosure.test.ts and the rendered-screen specs beside it. The real-wire lane cannot cover the whole journey because it neither mounts SecureStore-backed Settings screens nor sends a live credential to an external model provider; doing so would turn a test fixture into a production secret and a billable third-party call.

Someone opens the corpus-consent screen, finds every kind of material off and un-asked, turns their journal on, and later turns it back off -- which deletes the copies it collected and leaves a dated refusal on the record rather than an open question. Turning it on now reaches backwards as well: the entries already in their journal are sorted on the same terms as a new one, bounded so the request they are waiting on stays finite. The spec covers the switch and the deletion; what it cannot yet observe is the reach, because the lane has no classification provider, so a backfilled entry settles as unclassified and writes no fragment for a spec to see. A provider that refuses to bill now ends that reach rather than consuming the queue, and never costs the person the permission they just gave -- the switch still answers granted and the entries it did not get to keep their place. The backend pins it at backend/tests/test_corpus_consent_api.py.

Someone ends their account from inside the app: they read what goes and what stays, retype their own address to confirm, and the server erases them and hands back a receipt. The receipt's vault half is pinned to the answer a deployment WITH a vault owes them -- adepthood holds no purge verb on the vault contract, so it names what is left for them to run themselves. The lane is such a deployment because seed.upload-document needs somewhere to seed into, and `configured` is read from the deployment's own CREEK_VAULT_URL rather than from this account's connection.

A feature screen throws while a journal entry is on screen; the boundary shows the recovery card, "Try again" remounts the subtree, and the crash report that leaves the device carries none of what was written. Still uncovered because the e2e lane cannot mount a screen at all: it runs on the node environment with node_modules untransformed, so importing the boundary dies on @react-navigation/native's ESM and react-native's Flow syntax, and the lane's own guard pins the moduleNameMapper to the @/ alias so the React Native preset cannot be added to a spec. Observing the outgoing crash envelope is banned in this lane by the same guard. Covering it needs a second, rendering lane, not another spec here.

The server hits an unhandled exception while the journal shelf is loading; the app says something went wrong on our end and offers the server's request id as a reference, instead of telling the user to check their wifi. Each side is pinned separately: backend/tests/middleware/test_unhandled_exception_cors.py drives the real app and asserts the 500 leaves it carrying Access-Control-Allow-Origin, and src/api/__tests__/serverErrorIsNotOffline.test.ts asserts the client keeps the sanitised envelope's code and request id while a failure that produced no response at all reads as the server being unreachable. That last arm changed with #2661: a request a browser blocks on CORS and a request that reaches nothing are the same bare TypeError to JavaScript -- measured in Chromium, identical message, properties, and resource-timing entry -- so the copy no longer diagnoses the device, and the "you appear to be offline" claim is raised only behind the client's own connectivity signal. Both arms are pinned in src/api/__tests__/corsRejectionIsNotOffline.test.ts. Uncovered here because the real-wire lane has no way to make the live server 500 — every reachable failure is a deliberate 4xx or 503, and adding a fault-injection route to the production app to manufacture one would be worse than the gap.

A device that already holds one account's session is signed into by a second account without an explicit logout -- through the password-reset flow, or any path that reaches the login screen with a live cache on disk. The incoming user must see none of the previous user's habits, none of their check-in queue replayed under the new token, and none of their BYOK key on the resonance header. Uncovered because the leak is a row on the device rather than a row on the server: this lane drives HTTP against a live backend from Node, with no app process and therefore no AsyncStorage or SecureStore to seed, dirty, or read back, so a spec written against the wire could only assert that the backend scopes reads to its caller -- which it already did throughout, and which was never the failing half. Held meanwhile by src/context/__tests__/AccountSwitchWipe.integration.test.tsx, which drives the real AuthProvider and the real habitStorage against the in-memory AsyncStorage mock, plus the per-account namespacing tests in src/storage/__tests__/. The cold start behind that door is held by src/context/__tests__/ResumedSessionScope.integration.test.tsx, which pins the namespace a resumed session reads to the subject of the token it resumed rather than to a separately persisted stamp the two non-atomic sign-in writes can leave disagreeing.

A writer asks for resonance while the balance behind the key that pays for it is spent. What they got was "the AI provider is having trouble connecting, give it a moment and tap retry" -- a transient story for a permanent, billing-level refusal, so the retry button they were pointed at could never work and the real cause reached nobody. The journey now ends in copy that names the condition and the one action that clears it, split by whose key it was, with no retry affordance and the charge reversed; on the server's own key an operator gets the WARNING that is their first signal it happened at all. The browser spec presses "Get Resonance" against the real server for both halves -- the caller's own key (402) and, through the token-gated provider probe, the server's own key (503) -- and neither half raises the typed error: the lane points the production SDK clients at a loopback fake through their own OPENAI_BASE_URL / ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, so openai.RateLimitError and anthropic.BadRequestError are built by the SDKs out of the providers' real refusal bodies, which is the classification the bug turned on. The same spec drives the counterweight -- a genuine rate limit, same provider and same 429 with a different code, which keeps its transient copy and its retry -- proves an intimate page still reaches no provider with one armed, and reads walletaudit out of band to show the pass was charged and put back rather than never charged. Each side is still pinned separately: backend/tests/services/test_botmason_credit_exhausted.py drives both SDKs through a mock transport so each builds its own typed error from the provider's real body, backend/tests/test_resonance_endpoints.py asserts the 402/503 split and the operator record, and src/api/__tests__/errorMessages.test.ts asserts neither code inherits the transient copy.

Someone who made their own practice tag renames it, and later deletes it, from the recipe editor's tag library. The library could list and create and stopped there, so both routes were served, typed, and unreachable from any screen. The journey is the seam: that a rename reaches the row the client named and survives the next list rather than living in local state, that the slug a recipe step copied by value is untouched by it, that a shared tag refuses both mutations from the server rather than from what the client chose to render, and that deleting a personal tag leaves the shared library whole.

Someone writing a journal page -- including a Course reader writing a reflection, which is an ordinary page opened with a prefilled title -- taps "Photograph a page", photographs their handwritten response, and the transcription is appended into the entry they already had open rather than being filed as a second one. The seam is what makes that a single entry: the capture route hands the merged transcript back through an in-memory store and the open page's own create-then-update writer persists it, so the title and save context the writer arrived with survive and one POST /journal/ covers the whole journey. Uncovered because neither lane can drive the capture: the route auto-launches the device photo picker on mount, which the node lane cannot even mount (#2324) and which no browser spec has ever driven through a file chooser, and the transcription itself is a charged vision call that needs the lane's LLM stub wired through it.

A writer uses the same journal entry at 375px, the 600px two-column boundary, and 1200px. Live browser boxes prove Finish and Photograph a page remain on one unbroken rail without horizontal overflow; the wide secondary action keeps its camera and label inline, while constrained actions become icon-only without losing their accessible names. After the real autosave creates the entry and the writer pauses, Get Resonance is measured inside and centred on the wide marginalia column, its longest preflight state is held and measured within that fixed column, then the normal action is measured outside the margin in its narrow floating position. The journey makes a real curriculum reflection due, opens it through the shelf invitation, and measures the reflection-only Sources action beside Finish and Photograph at 600px, covering the worst-case three-control rail rather than inferring its geometry from component props.

Someone opens Past prompts from the journal shelf and reads the weekly questions they have already answered with what they wrote under each. Answering a prompt mirrors the response into the journal as an ordinary page, which keeps the writing and loses the question that drew it, so this route is the only one that returns the pair -- and nothing asked for it until this surface existed. What the seam has to prove is that a submitted response comes back joined to its own question, and that the limit and offset the modal sends actually slice the set rather than being ignored.

A person lets a habit rest during a Metta Return arc, then leaves the arc, and takes the habit up again from the Return surface -- no long-press on a locked tile, no 3-dot menu. The press is asserted on the server rather than on the card: the release row reads re-committed and the habit itself is unlocked again in the account's own habit list, which is the collection read that reconciles auto-reveals, so the pause is shown outranking the program's schedule while it holds and releasing it afterwards. That the row and not merely the habit recorded the re-commit is probed by locking the habit by hand from Habit Settings, which is the only thing that can tell the two halves of the reported flag apart. It runs in the browser lane because the journey is the card: the recovery affordance renders only on a shelf whose arc has ended while a release is outstanding, and the API lane cannot mount a React Native screen at all, so a spec there could only POST the route by hand. Deliberately under-claimed: only the recovery is pressed. Beginning the Return is its own journey (return.begin-a-return-from-the-journal-entry), and the let-go card that releases habits renders only in the session that started the arc, so release-then-leave is arranged over the same live wire -- every step read back, and Orange-stage eligibility asserted false before and true after the tests.e2e.program_anchor rewind, so an arrange that did nothing fails where it happened instead of leaving the press to test an empty shelf. The cross-tenant arm presses the same route from a second account holding an arc of its own: somebody else's habit id reads exactly like a nonexistent one, and the owner's own press afterwards proves that refusal is a refusal rather than a route that moves nothing. Verified to be a live gate: with recommit resolving the active arc again, as it did before the arc-spanning fix, the press 404s and the spec fails.

A journal entry whose resonance pass offers the Return is the card a person can begin one from: "Begin the Return" opens a confirmation naming the arc's five weekly foci as the server sent them, confirming opens an arc that lands on week one, and "Not now" persists the same decline the Journal shelf's offer card writes, so declining in the entry is honoured there. It runs in the browser lane because the journey is the card: the offer surfaces only while a resonance pass has just raised the in-memory contraction signal (src/store/useContractionSignalStore.ts) that useMettaReturn reads, and that store is fed by the screen's own pass -- the API lane cannot mount a screen at all, so a spec there could only call the two routes by hand. Both preconditions are arranged honestly: the contraction over the wire, from a habit whose foundation has been quiet past the detection window, and the Orange-stage eligibility by rewinding program_started_at through tests.e2e.program_anchor (no request schema accepts it) and then reading GET /stages, which is what records the entry -- eligibility is asserted false before and true after, so an arrange that did nothing fails rather than silently testing the simple_ease_off card. The double-tap latch is the one arm left to the Jest spec beside the component (src/features/Journal/__tests__/ContractionReflectionNote.test.tsx), which drives it deterministically; a browser cannot dispatch the second press without racing the first request. Verified to be a live gate: with confirmStart no longer calling start(), the spec fails on the arc POST that never leaves the browser.

A person whose reflections are still drawn from the last few days of writing is told so, in the sentence that is true for their own account: the consent decision if they have not made it, the import surface if they have. The band is declinable in one tap, renders no count, and never blocks resonance. The lane drives the two states and the move between them across the wire on its own account.

A writer can set aside the one-time explanation of where reflections come from without losing the corpus door. A cold reload proves the dismissal persists; the Journal drawer then remains the corpus's sole Journal surface, beside the icon-bearing Photograph a page action, and a fresh undecided account reaches the actual consent screen through a live GET /corpus/voice-readiness decision. The two mounted drawer hosts and the gathering-to-import arm are pinned in the adjacent component suites because the browser starts from only one readiness state.

A person sets a length on the journal's writing timer, writes until it runs out, is offered the session as a habit, and chooses where it sits among the habits they already signed up for — first position by default, with every other habit moving along one stage. The spec drives that write on its own account: it creates the habits the writer already had, then makes the placement the offer makes — one POST for the new habit carrying its stage and its place, one PUT per displaced row carrying theirs — and reads the list back. What only a live server can answer is whether the placement survives: that PUT /habits/{habit_id} keeps sort_order and stage instead of replacing them with the schema defaults, and that GET /habits/ then returns the rows in the order those numbers name, which is what makes the arrangement outlive a cold rehydrate. It also settles the lock: the row is created revealed=false like every other new habit, and the server's own one-shot reconciliation then opens it because Beige is a stage the writer has already reached — the spec pins both halves, and a habit at a stage they have not reached stays locked in the same pass. The offer's own rules (one-tap decline, a decline never re-asked, the stage preview) are pinned by the Jest specs beside WritingSessionOffer, and the offer's reachability from the writing page by JournalEntryScreenTimer.test.tsx; neither can cross the wire. What this spec cannot drive is the half-failure, because no live lane can refuse ONE displacing PUT in the middle of a fan-out: a POST that lands followed by a PUT that does not used to roll back the store alone, leaving a habit on the server the writer never confirmed under copy saying their habits were as they were. That branch is pinned beside habitManager instead (habitManager.test.ts: the created row is taken back off by the id its own POST returned; the branch where that DELETE is itself refused says the habit was saved out of place rather than reassuring; and a confirming re-fetch that fails after every write landed is not reported as a failed write).

A person finishes a timed writing session and is offered — beside the habit offer, under the same single decline — to keep it as the Journaling practice at Green. The offer describes what keeping it would do BEFORE it writes anything, because two things it would do are invisible from the journal page: Green may already hold a practice the writer chose (the server resolves a second open selection by closing the first, so a bare write evicts it silently), and Green may not be open to them yet (the selection is allowed as forward planning, but the just-finished session cannot be logged against it). This spec drives the server half on its own account, from a fresh signup standing at Beige — the harder half. It reads the seeded catalogue at stage 6 and pins that Journaling is there, approved, count_up, and twenty minutes; selects it at Green from Beige and pins that the server ACCEPTS the forward-planned pick, which is what makes the flow possible at all given that a mismatched stage_number is refused; pins that POST /practice-sessions/ against it is 403 stage_locked, which is why the client declines to send one and says so instead; reads the selection back by the effective_name the offer shows; and then puts another practice at Green and pins that the first row is CLOSED rather than the write refused — the silent eviction the offer names before the tap. The offer's own rules (one-tap decline, a decline never re-asked, the sentence shown before the write, no session claimed that was not logged) are pinned by the Jest specs beside WritingSessionOffer and SaveAsPracticeStep; none of them can cross the wire.

A user who already has habits reopens the scaffolding modal from the drawer or the energy footer and re-runs it. A habit they enter again keeps its own row: the new energy rating, icon, stage and staggered start date are PUT onto the id the server issued, while the streak, the check-ins, the goal ids and the unlock flag survive untouched. Before this, that pick was POSTed, the server rejected the duplicate name with a 409, the client swallowed it into a console line, and the rating the user had just confirmed was silently discarded while the stale row kept its old one -- only a habit under a genuinely new name ever appeared. A habit carried along from before the program is matched too, and stays on the negative lap with its own beginning rather than being scaffolded onto a program date. A habit the picks do not mention is retained, never released: the delete cascades that habit's goals and completions server-side and cannot be undone, so it follows only an explicit choice. That explicit release is implemented and unit-tested here -- deletes are awaited before any create, so a released name can be re-entered without the create hitting the same unique index -- and the review step now gives the user a way to state one, behind a confirmation that names the habit and says its check-ins and goals go with it. Uncovered because the seam runs through the habit service rather than the API client the lane drives directly: reaching it needs a lane that can open the modal, which is what the linked issue tracks. Pinned meanwhile by the "onboardingSave merge" block in src/features/Habits/services/__tests__/habitManager.test.ts, which drives the merge through the same bare picks the screen passes and asserts the exact create/update/delete call counts, the phase ordering, and that no fabricated id reaches the wire.

A person finishes a timed writing session, is offered that session as a habit inside the note the page leaves them, then starts a second session and abandons it partway. The offer is still there afterwards, still holding whatever they had chosen, and accepting it still saves the habit on their own account. That is the lifetime the note's children slot promises: an offer goes away only when the writer closes the note, or when a later session runs its full length and replaces the note with one about that newer session — never because a session was merely started, paused, or stopped early. The slot now holds a real offer, and both halves of the rule are pinned by the Jest specs beside WritingSessionSurface (WritingSessionOfferSlot.test.tsx: a standing offer survives an abandoned session, and is rebuilt when a newer session replaces the note). Still uncovered across the wire because the claim is about a mounted component surviving an interaction, and this lane runs on the node environment with node_modules untransformed and cannot mount a screen at all — the constraint #2324 records. The write the offer performs is covered end to end by journal.timed-writing-session-becomes-a-habit; what is missing is a rendering lane that can drive the surviving offer to it.

A user who already has habits opens Energy Scaffolding and is asked about them before anything else. Every habit they own is listed with a tick, ticked; for each ticked one they choose Bring along -- already mastered, tracked on the carryover pages -- or Re-rate, which puts it back in the pool to be rated and slotted into the new energy order with its stored ratings already on the sliders. Unticking one is how a habit is let go of, and it is the only irreversible thing on the step: continuing then names the habits by name and says their check-ins and goals go with them, and cancelling leaves every tick exactly where it was. Brought-along habits never reach the energy, reveal, reorder or template steps and never count against the ten-habit ceiling, so a user with ten habits who brings four along can still add four. Before this the modal opened on a blank page and whatever the user typed was appended beside everything they already had. Uncovered for the same reason as welcome.first-run-walkthrough-to-journal and habits.scaffolding-start-date-anchors-the-program: this lane runs on the node environment with node_modules untransformed and cannot mount a screen at all, and every step of this journey is inside a modal. Pinned meanwhile by src/features/Habits/components/__tests__/OnboardingModal.reviewStep.test.tsx, which drives the whole flow through the rendered modal to the plan the save receives, and by src/features/Habits/components/__tests__/onboardingReview.test.ts for the decisions themselves.

A user whose habits were created before sort_order existed holds NULL in every row. GET /habits/ used to order by sort_order ASC with no NULLS placement and no secondary key, so the order among those rows was undefined and PostgreSQL sorted them last -- the first numbered habit the user added leapfrogged every habit they had onboarded with, and because tile colour is positional (HabitsScreen colorIndices) the whole lap repainted around it. The list query now orders by sort_order ASC NULLS FIRST, then id: the unnumbered rows keep the head position they have always displayed in, a later numbered add lands after them, and the id key makes the order total even for a fully numbered store, where two rows may legitimately share a slot because slots restart at zero inside each is_carryover partition. Uncovered because the e2e lane cannot mint a pre-2026-09-02 store: the production client always stamps a slot on the rows it creates, so reaching the NULL population needs a fixture the lane has no seam for. Pinned meanwhile by backend/tests/test_habits_list_ordering.py, which asserts the ORDER BY the endpoint actually emitted, compiled to the PostgreSQL dialect -- the test lane is SQLite, which sorts NULLs first natively and cannot tell the fix from the defect.

A person deletes a habit they have actually used, and it stays deleted. The order is the finding: a habit created moments ago always deleted cleanly, and one that had ever been checked in returned 500, so this journey checks in on the clear goal, confirms the completion is really on the wire, and only then asks for the delete. The backend suite could not see this at all -- it runs on SQLite built from the model metadata, which until #2763 was not enforcing foreign keys, so a cascade that never ran and a cascade that ran perfectly left the same green. Here the schema is the migrated Postgres one and the four ON DELETE CASCADE constraints are the real ones. The re-read after the delete is what the reporter's next screen did: the symptom was a tile that came back, because the client reverts its optimistic removal when the server rejects.

Someone connects a private vault of their own from Settings: the screen reads whether one is attached, they paste an address and a key, the server refuses an address it cannot reach securely and writes no row for it, and a good one comes back connected with no credential on the reply. Both halves are green on their own — the screen's tests mock the client and the router's tests never build a request — so this is the one place they agree on the paths, the verbs, the refusal codes and the write-only credential. It pins four refusals rather than one -- an insecure transport, a destination only a local network can reach, an address that resolves nowhere, and a key no Authorization header could carry -- because the server judges where a URL points as well as how it is shaped, and the screen answers each with its own sentence.

An authenticated user chooses private-vault activation from Settings after signup, sees that it is optional and that INTIMATE processing is still unavailable, and explicitly starts an allocation. The production client crosses the live Adepthood API and Postgres lifecycle into an isolated fake Creek control plane, resumes at the client-held ceremony, submits only a protocol-shaped wrapped artifact after recovery acknowledgement, receives the one-way connection handoff, and renders the capability Creek actually verified rather than one inferred by the client. Unit journeys beside PrivateVaultActivationScreen pin the one-time recovery display, cancel-without-allocation, restart-without-secrets, accessibility, and web/iOS/Android recovery actions; this seam spec pins every route and schema between that screen and the two services.

A traveller reads a stage's subtitle -- the two-word label under its name -- on the Map modal, the Map's centre-cell accessibility label, the magnifier caption, and the Course cover. Every one of those renders stage.subtitle verbatim from GET /stages via stageService, and nothing is hardcoded client-side, which is exactly why the covering spec names no subtitle of its own: it reads the coursestage rows out of band, requires the served listing to match them stage for stage, then rewrites one row to a string the curriculum has never held and requires the client to follow it there -- an assertion that a route answering with its own copy of the seeded words cannot pass. What the server served is then fed through stageCenterCellLabel, the function MapScreen hands its centre cell, so the sentence a screen reader speaks is bound to the row too; the row is put back before the file ends. map.advance-stage opens the same screen against the same route but asserts the progress record (current_stage, completed_stages, stage_started_at) and never copy, so this journey keeps its own spec rather than widening that claim. #2577 corrected Teal's subtitle and was proven by a backend golden test, which pins the string at the source and says nothing about whether the client renders it.

A writer who has asked for reflections before asks for another one, and the Higher Self does not say a thing it has already said: at most two of the letters it wrote them earlier ride along with the pass as content-only context, under a pinned instruction never to imitate their wording or treat them as a voice sample. A letter about an entry they deleted, or one they later marked Intimate, is never among them, and neither is a letter about the page being read. Uncovered for the same reason as journal.ask-for-resonance and journal.see-related-vault-pages: what changes here is generated prose rather than a screen or a new seam, and the real-wire lane has no deterministic language-model provider, so it cannot make POST /journal/{entry_id}/resonance return notes it could read back and compare across two passes. #2408 tracks that missing provider seam. The exclusions are pinned end-to-end at the endpoint by backend/tests/test_intimate_privacy_guard.py::test_only_eligible_prior_letters_reach_the_cloud_prompt, and the query that decides them by backend/tests/test_prior_letters_grounding.py.

A writer presses OK on a completion-suggestion card in the journal margin and the accept is refused. The refusal is named where the writer is looking -- beside the very card that produced it, not in place of it -- and announced through a polite live region rather than only drawn, while the card stays pending and pressable so a second press really does check the habit off. The spec drives that over the real wire in a real browser: only the literary pass is intercepted, to reach a suggestion card without an LLM, while detection, the row, the refused accept, the retry and the persisted acceptance are all the live server. A 500 stands in for the class the margin used to swallow -- a 401, a 404, a 409 on an already-dismissed row, a request that never arrives -- because every one reaches the same catch. What no browser spec can reach is pinned beside it in Jest: src/features/Journal/__tests__/useResonance.test.tsx holds the copy to what the client can actually observe (a blocked preflight and an unreachable host are one bare TypeError), pins the habit-store refresh to the auth-hydrated zone rather than the device's, and pins that a success retires only its own card's complaint -- with two cards on screen, accepting one must not erase the other's still-live failure while that card is still pending.

Someone whose library has outgrown one page reads it whole. The client pages every list endpoint at fifty rows a page (api/index.ts, listAll -> fetchAllPages), and paginate_query used to apply OFFSET/LIMIT to whatever the router handed it and add no ordering of its own -- so GET /user-practices/ carried no ORDER BY at all, and neighbouring endpoints ordered on keys that tie (a practice-session timestamp, a recipe owner-and-name, a stageprogress user_id). OFFSET/LIMIT is only well-defined over a total order: inside a tie group the database may order each page request differently, so one selection can arrive on two consecutive pages while another arrives on none, and the reader sees a duplicate or a hole with nothing wrong in the store. paginate_query now appends the entity primary key to every page it serves, which is a no-op wherever the caller key was already total. Uncovered because the seam is a page boundary: this lane cannot mint the fifty-one rows that produce a second page without a fixture seam it has no route for, and even with one, an assertion on returned rows cannot tell the fix from the defect -- a planner is free to return the tie group in insertion order either way. Pinned meanwhile by backend/tests/test_pagination_total_order.py, which asserts the ORDER BY each endpoint actually emitted, compiled to the PostgreSQL dialect the test lane is not.

Someone whose Journaling practice is saved taps one button in the Practice player and lands on a blank journal page with the practice's own length already running; when the page's session ends it is recorded against that selection, and the "keep this as a practice?" offer is not put to them again. Uncovered because the one claim this adds over journal.timed-writing-session-becomes-a-practice is the COMPLEMENT of what that spec pins: that spec deliberately stands its account at Beige and proves POST /practice-sessions/ answers 403 stage_locked against a forward-planned Journaling selection at Green, which is why the launch sends nothing there. What is unproven end-to-end is the same request SUCCEEDING once Green has actually opened -- and reaching that state needs backend/tests/e2e/program_anchor.py to move the account's program anchor five stages back and a read of GET /stages/program-calendar to make the record catch up, then its own spec file, its own account via freshLicenseKey(), and e2eLaneGuard registration. Pinned meanwhile on the client side by src/features/Practice/__tests__/PracticeScreenQuickLaunch.test.tsx (the button exists only for a saved Journaling practice, and navigates with the override-aware length and the selection id) and src/features/Journal/__tests__/useQuickLaunchedSession.test.tsx (the finished session is recorded once, for the length actually written, and never sent when the stage is still ahead) -- both of which agree with themselves about a server that is not there.

A writer on the Journal shelf sets a stage prompt aside, finds it gone from the band and still gone after a cold start on a new session, brings it back, and is never told they skipped or failed anything. The invariant this crosses the wire for is the one a mocked test cannot see: a dismissal is a preference and never a completion, so the spec sets a prompt aside and then still writes a response to another prompt in the same week, proving the set-aside wrote no PromptResponse, marked nothing answered, did not move the reader's week and did not close the week to the prompts still standing. It also pins that the weekly prompt drawn from the same curriculum carries the same answer, that a repeated set-aside collapses onto the unique index rather than adding a second row, that undoing one that was never made is success, that an ordinal the stage does not carry and a stage the reader has not reached are refused exactly as the stage read refuses them, and -- the half a mis-scoped WHERE would make indistinguishable -- that one account's un-set-aside never removes another's, the prompt being named by curriculum position which is identical for everyone.

A practitioner opens Practice on a session whose one automatic GET /stages did not come back, and is told so instead of being shown stage 1 as though it were theirs. Practice takes a single stage-load attempt per session (#2002), and when it fails the store still holds its initial currentStage of 1 -- so the screen used to render that number silently, with the only in-app recovery being a trip to Map's retry. The spec fails the real listing at the wire, crosses to Practice through the drawer, and pins the three claims together: the number is named as a placeholder, the adopted practice underneath it is still on screen and still startable (this is a notice, not an error wall -- a person who only wants to sit is never gated), and lifting the failure and tapping Try again adds exactly ONE more request to the route and takes the notice away in the same page load. That last count is the half no mocked suite can make: it is the guard from #2002 -- automatic attempts stay at one, the retry is the deliberate second -- measured against a real server rather than against a stub that agrees with itself.

A user completes a habit, leaves the app open across their local midnight, and looks again: the habit reads as not-yet-done today, its tier stars return to unlit, and the journal shelf's "Today's habits" count is back to zero -- with nothing remounted and no completion rewritten. Returning to the Habits tab or the shelf also re-reads habits from the server rather than showing whatever the store held when the tab was first opened. Uncovered because neither half is reachable from this lane: the rollover is clock-driven and crosses no wire at all -- that is the point of it, since only what is re-derived changes -- and the node environment cannot mount a screen to advance a clock against, the same constraint recorded on welcome.first-run-walkthrough-to-journal. The focus half does cross the wire but needs a real navigator the user can leave and return to. Jest pins both halves in process today, against a real NavigationContainer and against fake timers advanced past local midnight; covering this needs the browser lane, which can install a fake clock on the mounted app. See #2771.
